title: The ragas close
hookLine: the walk through the Granth's ragas ends: dusk, dawn, spring, rain and a serious morning, all carrying one Word

lines: WHAT RAN THROUGH ALL OF THEM?
cards: Watch one river from the same bridge all day. Gray and quick at dawn. Brown and slow at noon.
Gold at evening, then black, with lights on it. Someone passing at each hour could think it was a different river. It's one water, wearing the hours.
Since the day this path asked why the Granth is sung, it has walked raga by raga through the pages. Today the ragas close, and the question is what ran through all of them.

teach.h: FROM WHY IT'S SUNG TO JAIJAVANTI.
teach.b: Look back at the road. It began with why the Granth is sung at all, then the small markings, ghar and rahao, then strings and drums, then the order of the ragas.

Then Sri Rag, Majh, Gauri, Asa, and on through the book: Sorath and Bilaval, Ramkali and Maru, Tukhari's months, Kedara's dusk, Bhairao's serious morning, Basant's spring, Malar's rain, Kanara, Kalyan's evening, Prabhati's dawn, and Jaijavanti, where the ragas end.
Then the Ragmala, held with respect in two ways, the ragis who keep the old tunes alive, and the raga that feels like yours.

teach.h: EVERY SECTION POINTS TO THE NAME.
teach.b: Each section opens under its own heading, with an invocation of the One, and every one holds hymns that point the same way: toward the Name, the Word, the Shabad. The moods changed. The Word didn't.
Guru Nanak has a line in the Japji that fits. In paraphrase: with a single word, the Creator spread out the expanse of creation, and from it rivers beyond counting flowed.
One word; many rivers. The Gurus didn't write a different faith for the morning and another for the evening.
They set the one Word in mood after mood, so it could meet a person wherever they were: tender at dusk, hopeful in spring, heavy-hearted on a hard morning, quiet before dawn.
So when you hear kirtan from now on, the raga name at the top isn't a puzzle to solve.

teach.h: THE HOUR THE WORD HAS DRESSED FOR.
teach.b: It's the hour the Word has dressed for.
Tomorrow a new stretch begins: Guru Nanak's conversation on a mountain, recorded in Ramkali.

how: Sikhs hear the Granth's ragas in kirtan through the day and the year, with different ragas for different hours and seasons, all of them carrying Gurbani, the Guru's Word.

o: the closing hymn sung to end each evening's kirtan
the moment a raga's final note fades into silence
the end of the raga road, where every mood points to one Word

games.q: the block in moods — tap the pairs.

s: each raga section of the Granth teaches a different faith
the moods change; every section points to the same Name and Word.
in the Japji, Guru Nanak says the expanse of creation came from a single word
with one word the Creator spread it out, and rivers beyond counting flowed.

games.q: the ragas are done. you're asked what ran through all of them, dusk to dawn to the last raga. what do you say?
o: the one Word, set in mood after mood.
games.why: every section opens with its own heading and points to the Name; one word, many rivers, as the Japji puts it.

practice: If you can, play a shabad in a raga you skipped or barely lingered on, and let it be unfamiliar, noticing the mood it brings, without naming it too fast.
Then, under the mood, listen for the steady thing: the breath going in and out, the same as in every other raga.
If you pray, let the Word, Waheguru, be the river under the changing light; if you don't, let the breath be that river, one water through every hour.

wordCard.voice: The ragas close. The end of the walk through the Granth's ragas, where every section, in every mood, points to one Word. Today's word.

orig.note: shabad: the Word, and a hymn of the Granth; the one thing every raga carries.

carryVoice: Your line: many moods, one word. The river changes color all day and stays one water. One stretch done, and the hill goes on.
